question: How do I connect to the SWC HPC cluster from my laptop?

tries.answer:
## Connecting to the SWC HPC cluster from your laptop

**Prerequisites:** an SWC account (username + password) and an SSH client (pre-installed on Linux/macOS; on Windows the docs recommend installing [Git Bash](https://gitforwindows.org/) so all the commands in the guide work as written).

### If you're outside the SWC network

You must first hop through the *bastion* node (`sgw2`), then on to the *gateway* node (`hpc-gw2`):

```console
$ ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
<SWC-USERNAME>@sgw2:~$ ssh hpc-gw2
<SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2:~$
```

### If you're at SWC on a wired connection (not eduroam), or on the SWC VPN

You can go straight to the gateway:

```console
$ ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2.hpc.swc.ucl.ac.uk
```

Type `exit` to undo the last `ssh` hop and return.

### Make it one command

Add this to `~/.ssh/config` on your laptop (for connecting from *outside* the network):

```bash
# Specify our intermediate jump host, aka the bastion node
Host swc-bastion
    HostName ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
    User <SWC-USERNAME>

# Specify how to get to the gateway node by jumping through the bastion node
Host swc-gateway
    HostName hpc-gw2
    User <SWC-USERNAME>
    ProxyJump swc-bastion
```

Then `ssh swc-gateway` gets you there in one step (and `exit` once returns you to your laptop).

### Skip the password

```console
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519
$ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub swc-gateway
```

Your SWC home directory is shared across all HPC nodes, so the key works everywhere. The SSH-keys section is the one part the docs say Windows users can't follow with native Windows tools — use Git Bash for it.

### Once you're on the gateway

Use it only for navigating the filesystem, editing scripts (`nano`/`vim`), and submitting jobs — don't run computations there, since it's shared. Request a compute node instead, e.g.:

```console
$ srun -p cpu -n 4 --mem 8G --pty bash -i
```

Source: [Set up SSH for the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SSH-SWC-cluster.md)

From **"Set up SSH for the SWC HPC cluster"** ([link](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SSH-SWC-cluster.md)):

## Prerequisites
An SWC account (username + password from SWC IT), and an SSH client — pre-installed on Linux and macOS. On Windows the guide recommends installing [Git Bash](https://gitforwindows.org/) so all the commands work as written (Windows 10+ can also use `cmd`/PowerShell natively for everything except the SSH-keys section).

## Logging in
Which route you take depends on where your laptop is:

**At SWC on a wired connection (not eduroam), or on the SWC VPN** — connect straight to the *gateway* node:
```console
$ ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2.hpc.swc.ucl.ac.uk
```

**Anywhere else (off-network)** — hop via the *bastion* node first:
```console
$ ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
<SWC-USERNAME>@sgw2:~$ ssh hpc-gw2
```
The password won't be displayed as you type. `exit` undoes the last `ssh`.

Note the addresses differ from the hostnames you land on (`ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk` → `sgw2`); check your prompt or run `hostname` to see where you are.

## Make it one command
Add aliases to `~/.ssh/config` on your laptop (this config is for connecting from *outside* the network):

```bash
# Specify our intermediate jump host, aka the bastion node
Host swc-bastion
    HostName ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
    User <SWC-USERNAME>

# Specify how to get to the gateway node by jumping through the bastion node
# The gateway hostname is specified as the jump-host would see it
Host swc-gateway
    HostName hpc-gw2
    User <SWC-USERNAME>
    ProxyJump swc-bastion
```

Then `ssh swc-gateway` gets you there in one step. To skip the password too, generate a key with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` and copy it over with `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub swc-gateway` — your SWC home directory is shared across all nodes, so the key works everywhere.

## Once you're on
The gateway is a *staging area* only — filesystem navigation, editing scripts with `nano`/`vim`, and job submission. Don't run computations there; request a compute node via SLURM, e.g.:
```console
$ srun -p cpu -n 4 --mem 8G --pty bash -i
```

question: How do I ask for a GPU in a SLURM batch script?

tries.answer:
Use the `--gres` directive — and note you must also be on the `gpu` partition:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH -J my_job              # job name
#SBATCH -p gpu                 # partition (queue)
#SBATCH -N 1                   # number of nodes
#SBATCH --mem 16G              # memory pool for all cores
#SBATCH -n 4                   # number of cores
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00             # time (D-HH:MM)
#SBATCH --gres gpu:1           # request 1 GPU (of any kind)
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out  # STDOUT
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err  # STDERR
```

Key points from the docs:

- **No GPU is allocated unless you pass `--gres`**, even if you submitted to the `gpu` partition.
- `--gres gpu:1` gives you 1 GPU of any kind.
- To request a specific type, include its name: `--gres gpu:rtx2080:1`, `--gres gpu:rtx5000:1`, `--gres gpu:a100_2g.10gb:1`.
- Available GPU types are listed on the SWC internal wiki (linked from the page below); `sinfo` on the cluster shows partitions, their nodes and time limits.

Source: [SLURM arguments primer](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/SLURM-arguments.md)

Use the `--gres` directive — and note you also need the `gpu` partition.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

#SBATCH -J my_job            # job name
#SBATCH -p gpu               # partition (queue)
#SBATCH -N 1                 # number of nodes
#SBATCH --mem 16G            # memory pool for all cores
#SBATCH -n 4                 # number of cores
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00           # time (D-HH:MM)
#SBATCH --gres gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (of any kind)
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
```

Key points from the docs:

- **`--gres` is required.** No GPU is allocated to you unless you ask for it with `--gres`, *even if you are on the `gpu` partition*.
- **Any GPU:** `--gres gpu:1`
- **A specific type:** include its name, e.g. `--gres gpu:rtx2080:1`. Other example values given: `gpu:rtx5000:1`, `gpu:a100_2g.10gb:1`.

question: I'm running Jupyter on a cluster node. How do I open it in my browser?

tries.answer:
SSH port forwarding from the compute node to your laptop. The docs cover exactly this for the SWC cluster:

**1. On the node (inside your SLURM interactive job)** — launch Jupyter on a chosen port with no browser:

```bash
jupyter lab --no-browser --port=8082
```

Note the node name you were assigned (e.g. `gpu-sr670-20`), and keep the output line under *"Or copy and paste one of these URLs:"* — you need the full URL including `?token=…`.

**2. On your local machine**, in a separate terminal, open the tunnel through the bastion and gateway:

```bash
ssh -N <SWC-USERNAME>@<node-name> -J <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk,<SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2 -L 8082:localhost:8082
```

**3. In your browser**, paste the complete URL Jupyter printed, e.g. `http://localhost:8082/lab?token=abc123…`. The token is what authenticates you.

Troubleshooting from the page: use the same port in both commands; if the port is in use try another (`8888`, `8090`) in *both*; and keep the SLURM session on the node alive or the connection drops.

The guide also notes it deliberately avoids SSHing into unallocated nodes — you only tunnel to a node SLURM assigned you.

Source: [Accessing HTTP servers on the HPC with port forwarding](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/port-forwarding.md)

Use SSH port forwarding from the compute node to your laptop. The docs cover exactly this (assuming the SWC HPC cluster):

**1. Launch Jupyter on the node you were assigned by SLURM** (don't SSH into unallocated nodes). From an interactive job, e.g.:

```bash
srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --mem=16G --pty bash -i
conda activate my_env
cd /path/to/your/project
jupyter lab --no-browser --port=8082
```

Keep the output — you need the lines under "Or copy and paste one of these URLs:", which include the `?token=...`.

**2. In a separate terminal on your local machine**, tunnel that port through the bastion and gateway:

```bash
ssh -N <SWC-USERNAME>@<node-name> \
  -J <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk,<SWC-USERNAME>@hpc-gw2 \
  -L 8082:localhost:8082
```

Replace `<node-name>` with the node SLURM actually gave you (e.g. `gpu-sr670-20`).

**3. Paste the full Jupyter URL into your browser**, token included:

```
http://localhost:8082/lab?token=abc123def456...
```

Troubleshooting from the page: use the same port in both commands; if the port is in use try another (e.g. `8888`, `8090`) in both; and keep the SLURM session on the node alive or the connection drops.

Page: [Accessing HTTP servers on the HPC with port forwarding](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/port-forwarding.md)

question: How do I train a SLEAP model on the SWC cluster?

tries.answer:
The NIU how-to guide covers exactly this: **[Use SLEAP on the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/data_analysis/HPC-module-SLEAP.md)**. The workflow splits into two halves: prepare locally in the SLEAP GUI, train on the cluster via SLURM.

## 1. Prerequisites

- Cluster access: `ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk`, then `ssh hpc-gw2`.
- Check the module: `module avail SLEAP`. `module load SLEAP` gives the default `SLEAP/2026-05-08` (SLEAP v1.6.3, PyTorch backend) — recommended for new projects. Older modules use the legacy TensorFlow backend.
- Install SLEAP locally too (you need the GUI for labelling), matching the module version. For the current default:
  ```
  uv tool install --python 3.13 "sleap[nn]==1.6.3" --with "sleap-io==0.7.0" --with "sleap-nn==0.2.0" --torch-backend auto
  ```
- Keep your data on `ceph` (the cluster has fast access to it) and mount the SWC filesystem locally.

If you have an IT-managed Linux desktop, you can skip the prerequisites and just `module load SLEAP` there — though you'd still offload GPU work to the cluster.

## 2. Prepare the training job (local GUI)

Label frames per the SLEAP tutorial, saving the project (e.g. `labels.v002.slp`) on the mounted SWC filesystem. Then **don't hit Run** — instead: *Predict* → *Run Training…* → *Export Training Job Package…*, with *Inference Target* set to *Nothing*. Save the `.zip` on ceph and unzip it; the folder holds the YAML configs and a `.pkg.slp` labels file.

## 3. Write a SLURM script

Create `train-slurm.sh` **inside the training job folder** (the commands use relative paths):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J slp_train
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --mem 32G
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00
#SBATCH --gres gpu:a100:1
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=user@domain.com

nvidia-smi
module load SLEAP

sleap train --config-name centroid.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
sleap train --config-name centered_instance.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
```

Two `sleap train` calls here because the example uses the Top-Down config (centroid + centered_instance); your config files depend on what you chose in the GUI.

Two cautions the guide flags:
- `--ntasks-per-node=1` is required — PyTorch Lightning needs that form rather than `--ntasks`/`-n`.
- Don't copy `train-script.sh` verbatim: it may reference paths from the exporting machine, and a `trainer_config.run_name=...` value containing `=` makes SLEAP fail with `mismatched input '=' expecting`.

For GPU types, `sinfo -p gpu,gpu_lowp -o "%N %G" --noheader` lists what's available; avoid `p5000` cards (compute capability too low for PyTorch ≥ 2.5). `--gres gpu:1` requests any GPU.

## 4. Submit and monitor

```console
$ cd /path/to/labels.v002.slp.training_job
$ sbatch train-slurm.sh
$ squeue --me          # or sacct, or cat slurm.*.out / .err
```

## 5. Evaluate

A `models/` folder appears in the training job folder, one subfolder per run (e.g. `260512_151547.centroid.n=46`) containing `best.ckpt`, `training_config.yaml` and metrics. View them in the local GUI via *Predict* → *Evaluation Metrics for Trained Models…*.

The same page continues into inference (`sleap track` in an `infer-slurm.sh` script), the training–inference refinement cycle, and troubleshooting (`srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash -i` then `sleap doctor` to confirm GPU access). On legacy TensorFlow modules the CLI is `sleap-train`/`sleap-track` with JSON configs instead — see the page's legacy section.

Here's the workflow from the NIU how-to guide, which documents the current PyTorch-based module (`SLEAP/2026-05-08`, SLEAP v1.6.3).

## 1. Prepare the job locally (SLEAP GUI)

Label frames following the SLEAP tutorial, saving the project file (e.g. `labels.v002.slp`) on the mounted SWC filesystem — not your local disk. Then **don't press `Run`** in the training dialog. Instead: *Predict* → *Run Training…* → **Export Training Job Package…**

- Set *Inference Target* to **Nothing** (run training and inference separately on the cluster).
- Save the `.training_job.zip` on the SWC filesystem, then unzip it. The folder contains the YAML configs, a packaged labels file (`.pkg.slp`), and SLEAP's own `train-script.sh`.
- Keep your local SLEAP version matched to the cluster module.

Data must live on `ceph` for fast cluster access — `rsync` it over if not.

## 2. Log in and go to the job folder

```console
$ ssh <SWC-USERNAME>@ssh.swc.ucl.ac.uk
$ ssh hpc-gw2
$ cd /ceph/.../labels.v002.slp.training_job
```

The guide warns against running the exported `train-script.sh` verbatim: its paths may point at the machine that exported the package, and its `trainer_config.run_name=...` value can contain an `=` sign, making SLEAP fail with `mismatched input '=' expecting`. Write the `sleap train` commands yourself instead.

## 3. Write `train-slurm.sh` inside the job folder

Inside that folder, because the commands use relative paths:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J slp_train
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --mem 32G
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH -t 0-06:00
#SBATCH --gres gpu:a100:1
#SBATCH -o slurm.%x.%N.%j.out
#SBATCH -e slurm.%x.%N.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=user@domain.com

nvidia-smi
module load SLEAP

sleap train --config-name centroid.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
sleap train --config-name centered_instance.yaml --config-dir . trainer_config.ckpt_dir='models'
```

Notes from the guide:
- One `sleap train` call per model — the example is a Top-Down config (centroid + centered_instance); your config files depend on what you chose.
- `--ntasks-per-node=1` is required: PyTorch Lightning needs this form rather than `--ntasks`/`-n`, and manages GPU parallelism within that process.
- No `cuda` module needed — PyTorch bundles its own runtime.
- For any GPU use `--gres gpu:1`; list available types with `sinfo -p gpu,gpu_lowp -o "%N %G" --noheader` and avoid compute capability < 7.5 (currently only `p5000`).

## 4. Submit and monitor

```console
$ sbatch train-slurm.sh
$ squeue --me        # or sacct, or cat slurm.*.out / slurm.*.err
```

For OOM errors: `--mem` controls CPU RAM; GPU memory comes from the card type you request, so ask for a bigger one (e.g. `a100`) or shrink the model (backbone, input scaling, max stride, batch size).

## 5. Evaluate

A `models/` folder appears with one subfolder per run (e.g. `260512_151547.centroid.n=46`) holding `best.ckpt`, `training_config.yaml`, `metrics.*.npz`. In the local GUI: *Predict* → *Evaluation Metrics for Trained Models…* → *Add Trained Model(s)* → *View Metrics*.

If something's broken, test with an interactive GPU job — `srun -p gpu --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash -i`, then `nvidia-smi`, `module load SLEAP`, `sleap doctor`.

Source: [Use SLEAP on the SWC HPC cluster](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/data_analysis/HPC-module-SLEAP.md) — it also covers inference (`sleap track`), the training–inference cycle, and legacy TensorFlow modules (`sleap-train` with JSON configs).

question: How do I pull template updates into a project I made with the NIU cookiecutter?

tries.answer:
Use **cruft**. The NIU how-to covers exactly this.

## First-time setup — `cruft link`

```bash
pip install cruft
cruft link https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/python-cookiecutter
```

Cruft re-asks the cookiecutter questions. Give the same answers as when you generated the repo, **except** enter `provide later` for `github_repository_url` — the docs note that entering your real repo URL there makes `cruft diff` fail.

Then it prompts for the commit hash of the cookiecutter version you originally generated from. You have to find this manually in the template's history (the docs' example: `9daec12bffbc32da6a252605c5e67c90028fefc0`). Cruft only updates files changed since that commit.

This writes a `.cruft.json` (template URL, commit hash, your answers) — track it in git.

## Pulling updates — `cruft diff` / `cruft update`

```bash
cruft diff     # see what differs from the template
cruft update   # apply; confirm with y, or press v to view first
cruft check    # boolean: up to date or not
```

Caveats from the page:
- `cruft update` won't delete files you added since creation, and won't delete files removed from the template — do those by hand.
- Conflicts produce a `your_file.rej` per file; apply those changes manually and delete the `.rej` files afterwards.
- `.cruft.json` gets the new commit hash, so future updates build on it.

Finally, commit to a branch, open a PR into `main`, and check CI before merging.

Source: [Update cookiecutter-generated files with cruft](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/Cookiecutter-cruft.md)

Use **`cruft`**. Install with `pip install cruft`.

**First time only — `cruft link`:**

```bash
cruft link https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/python-cookiecutter
```

- It re-asks the same cookiecutter questions — give the same answers as before, **except** enter `provide later` for `github_repository_url` (the docs note that giving the real URL makes `cruft diff` fail).
- Then it asks for the commit hash of the template version you originally generated from — you have to find this manually in the template's history (the page's example: `9daec12bffbc32da6a252605c5e67c90028fefc0`).
- This creates `.cruft.json` (template URL, commit hash, your answers). Track it in git.

**Then, to update:**

```bash
cruft diff     # see what differs from the template
cruft update   # apply; confirm with y, or press v to view first
cruft check    # boolean: up to date or not
```

Caveats from the page:
- `cruft update` won't delete files you added, nor files that were removed from the template — remove those yourself.
- Conflicts produce a `your_file.rej` per file; apply those by hand and delete the `.rej` files afterwards.
- `.cruft.json` gets the new commit hash after a successful update, so the next one starts from there.

Finally, commit on a new branch, open a PR into `main`, and check the GitHub Actions pass before merging.

Source: [Update cookiecutter-generated files with cruft](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/programming/Cookiecutter-cruft.md)

question: Which licence should I choose for my research software?

tries.answer:
**The NIU recommendation: [BSD-3-Clause](https://opensource.org/licenses/BSD-3-Clause)** — unless your software has commercial potential or depends on other software with a restrictive licence. It allows virtually unrestricted use while including a liability disclaimer.

Before settling on it, the guide asks you to work through these checks:

1. **Confirm you may license it** — usually your group leader's or department head's call.
2. **Get permission from other contributors**, in writing if any part was developed at another institute, and respect their institution's/funders' requirements. Easiest if you pick a licence *before* starting work.
3. **Commercial potential?** Contact your institutional IP/tech-transfer team (e.g. [UCL Business](https://www.uclb.com/)) *before* releasing the code.
4. **Check funder/institute policy** — at the time of writing, UCL, Gatsby and Wellcome have no formal OSS licensing policy.
5. **Check your dependencies' licences** and release in accordance with them.
6. **Consider what others in the field use** — compatible licences make it easier to join a wider ecosystem of tools.
7. If you have specific requirements, use a guide like [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/) or [tldrlegal.com](https://tldrlegal.com/); otherwise go with BSD-3-Clause.

Don't write your own licence (e.g. "academic use only") unless you're an IP lawyer — established licences let others understand the terms without seeking legal advice.

**Adding it:** copy the licence text into a file named `LICENSE.txt` (or similar) and ship it with your software. On GitHub, creating a new file called `LICENSE.txt` via the web interface gives you a "Choose a license template" button with a list to pick from.

Two things worth knowing: you *can* change the licence later, but earlier versions stay under the original terms. And if you merely call a GPL-family library installed separately (e.g. a Python package), you can license normally — but bundling or linking against it may constrain your choice, so check that specific licence's terms.

Source: [Software licensing — NIU how-to guides](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/Licensing.md). Note the page's own disclaimer: it wasn't written by lawyers and isn't legal advice or official SWC/GCNU/UCL guidance.

The NIU how-to guide on software licensing has a direct recommendation:

**Unless your software has commercial potential or depends on other software with a restrictive licence, use the [3-Clause BSD License (BSD-3-Clause)](https://opensource.org/licenses/BSD-3-Clause)** — a simple licence allowing virtually unrestricted use, with a liability disclaimer.

Before you settle on it, the guide asks you to work through these checks:

1. Make sure you have permission to license the software — usually your research group leader's or department head's decision.
2. Get permission from any other contributors, in writing if any part was developed at another institute. Changing a licence later with external collaborators involved is tricky, so choose early.
3. If you think the software has commercial potential, contact your institutional IP / tech transfer team (e.g. UCL Business) **before** releasing the code.
4. Follow funder and institutional requirements. For SWC/GCNU researchers, the guide notes UCL, Gatsby and Wellcome had no formal OSS licensing policy at the time of writing.
5. Check the licences of your dependencies and release in accordance with them.
6. Consider what other software in your field uses — compatible licences make it easier to contribute to a wider ecosystem.
7. For specific requirements, consult [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/) or [tldrlegal.com](https://tldrlegal.com/). Otherwise, BSD-3-Clause.

Two further points worth knowing:

- **Don't write your own licence** (including academic-use-only ones) unless you're an IP lawyer — established licences let others understand the terms without seeking legal advice.
- **Adding it** is just copying the licence text into a file named `LICENSE.txt` alongside your software. On GitHub, creating a new file named `LICENSE.txt` through the web interface gives you a "Choose a license template" button with a list to pick from.
- **GPL dependencies:** if the library is installed separately and you simply call it (e.g. a Python package), you can licence your code as normal. If you bundle or link against it, check that specific licence's terms — the GPL family (GPL, LGPL, AGPL) varies.

Note the guide's own disclaimer: it wasn't written by lawyers and isn't legal advice or official SWC/GCNU/UCL guidance.

question: How do I publish a dataset on GIN?

tries.answer:
Here's the workflow from the NIU how-to guide.

## One-time setup
1. Create a [GIN account](https://gin.g-node.org/user/sign_up).
2. Download the GIN CLI and log in: `gin login` (prompts for username/password).
3. Check it works: `gin --version`

## Create the repository and upload the data

Log in first (`gin login`), then:

**New directory:**
```
gin create <repository-name>
```
This creates the repo on the GIN server under your account plus a local directory of the same name — then move/copy your data files in.

**Existing directory** (`cd` into it first):
```
gin create --here <repository-name>
```

Then record and upload:
```
gin commit --message <message> <filename>
gin upload <filename>
```
`<filename>` can be a wildcard (`*.png`), a whitespace-separated list, or `.` for all changed files. You can commit several times and upload once. Note that `gin upload` syncs *all* changes including deletions — deleting a file locally and uploading removes it from the server too.

Useful: `gin ls` for status, `gin sync` for bidirectional sync, `gin remotes` to list remotes (`gin upload --to <remote-name>` targets one).

## Make it public

**New GIN repos are private by default.** To publish:
1. Go to the remote repo's homepage (`gin repos --all` lists your URLs).
2. Click *Settings* (top right).
3. Unselect the *Private* checkbox under *Basic settings*.

## Consider locking the files

For a dataset meant as a read-only archive, the GIN docs recommend keeping files **locked** (`gin lock <filename>`) — it saves storage since content isn't duplicated between the working directory and the git annex. Keep them unlocked only if you need to edit large files and snapshot progress. Files must be committed before locking, and you need another `gin commit` afterwards to record the lock state.

Source: [Create a GIN repository for your dataset](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/GIN-repositories.md)

One thing this page doesn't cover: if by "publish" you mean formally depositing a dataset alongside a paper (DOI, repository choice), there's a separate [Data sharing](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/Data-sharing.md) guide — say the word and I'll read it.

Publishing a dataset on GIN is: create a repo, upload your files, then make it public.

**One-off setup**
1. Create [a GIN account](https://gin.g-node.org/user/sign_up).
2. Download the GIN CLI and log in: `gin login` (prompts for username and password).
3. Check it works: `gin --version`

On MacOS/Ubuntu you may need `sudo` for some `gin` commands.

**Create the repository**

Log in first with `gin login`, then either:

- New directory: `gin create <repository-name>` — creates the repo on the GIN server under your account plus a directory of the same name locally; then move or copy your data into it.
- Existing directory: `cd` there and run `gin create --here <repository-name>` — creates the remote repo and links it to the current directory.

(Alternatively create it [in the browser](https://gin.g-node.org/repo/create) and `gin get <username>/<remote-repository-name>`; or `gin init` plus `gin add-remote <remote-name> <remote-repository-location>`.)

**Upload the data**

```
gin commit --message <message> <filename>
gin upload <filename>
```

`<filename>` can be a wildcard (`*.png`), a whitespace-separated list, or `.` for everything changed. Uncommitted changes in the file set are committed automatically on upload. Note that `gin upload` sends *all* changes including deletions and renames — deleting locally and uploading removes the file from the server too. Use `gin ls` to check status and `gin sync` to sync both ways.

**Make it public** — new repos are private by default:
1. Go to the remote repo's homepage (`gin repos --all` lists your URLs).
2. Click *Settings* (top right).
3. Unselect the *Private* checkbox under *Basic settings*.

**Then consider file locking.** For a dataset meant as a read-only archive, the docs recommend keeping files **locked** (`gin lock <filename>`, then `gin commit` to record the state change) — this saves storage, since unlocked files with content downloaded exist both in the working directory and the git annex. Keep files unlocked only if your workflow needs to edit large files and snapshot progress.

One thing the page doesn't cover: formal publication in the sense of minting a DOI / registering the dataset. It only describes creating a repo and making it public. For that you'd need to check GIN's own docs.

Source: [Create a GIN repository for your dataset](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/neuroinformatics-unit/blob/29043ff0fe2692cddca11ee573d8a4e1ba263ecd/docs/source/howto/open_science/GIN-repositories.md)

question: How do I load DeepLabCut or SLEAP tracks into movement?

tries.answer:
Both are supported pose formats. The docs give two routes.

**Unified loader (recommended)**

```python
from movement.io import load_dataset

# source_software defaults to "auto" (inferred from the file format)
ds = load_dataset("/path/to/file.h5", source_software="auto", fps=30)

# or be explicit
ds = load_dataset("/path/to/file.csv", source_software="DeepLabCut", fps=30)
```

Passing `fps` makes the time coordinate seconds rather than frame numbers. For DeepLabCut-style `.csv` (also used by LightningPose) the ambiguity is recorded in `ds.attrs["source_software"]` as `"DeepLabCut/LightningPose"` unless you set `source_software` yourself.

**Software-specific loaders**

```python
from movement.io import load_poses

# DeepLabCut: .h5 or .csv, or a DLC-style DataFrame
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.h5", fps=30)
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_style_df(df, fps=30)

# SLEAP: analysis .h5 (recommended)
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.analysis.h5", fps=30)
# .slp is experimental
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.predictions.slp", fps=30)
```

Caveats the page flags:

- Only **tracked predictions** are supported — manually labelled data (non-continuous frames) is not.
- For DeepLabCut, all individuals must share the same keypoint set; maDLC projects with per-individual keypoints aren't supported.
- SLEAP `.analysis.h5` is preferred over `.slp`.

To try it without your own files, `sample_data.list_datasets()` / `sample_data.fetch_dataset("SLEAP_three-mice_Aeon_proofread.analysis.h5")`.

Source: [movement — Input/Output](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/movement/blob/v0.18.0/docs/source/user_guide/input_output.md)

## The unified loader (recommended)

```python
from movement.io import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("/path/to/file.h5", source_software="auto", fps=30)
```

`source_software="auto"` is the default — movement infers it from the file format via `infer_source_software`. Passing `fps` puts time coordinates in seconds rather than frame numbers. You can pin the loader explicitly when you know the source (or when the format is ambiguous — DeepLabCut-style `.csv` is also used by LightningPose, in which case the inferred value is recorded as `ds.attrs["source_software"] = "DeepLabCut/LightningPose"`):

```python
ds = load_dataset("/path/to/file.csv", source_software="DeepLabCut", fps=30)
```

Use `movement.io.load.get_supported_source_software()` to list what's loadable.

## Software-specific functions

```python
from movement.io import load_poses

# DeepLabCut — .h5 or .csv
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.h5", fps=30)
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_file("/path/to/file.csv", fps=30)
ds = load_poses.from_dlc_style_df(df, fps=30)        # a DLC-style DataFrame

# SLEAP — analysis .h5 (recommended) or .slp (experimental)
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.analysis.h5", fps=30)
ds = load_poses.from_sleap_file("/path/to/file.predictions.slp", fps=30)
```

Either way you get a movement poses dataset with the trajectories, per-point confidence values, and metadata attributes.

Two caveats the page flags: movement only works with *tracked* predictions (identities continuous across frames) — manually labelled data isn't supported; and all individuals must share the same keypoint set, so multi-animal DLC projects with per-individual keypoints aren't supported.

## Trying it without your own data

```python
from movement import sample_data

print(*sample_data.list_datasets(), sep="\n")
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset("SLEAP_three-mice_Aeon_proofread.analysis.h5")
```

Source: [movement — Input/Output](https://github.com/neuroinformatics-unit/movement/blob/v0.18.0/docs/source/user_guide/input_output.md)

question: How do I install the BrainGlobe tools?

tries.answer:
Install into a virtual environment (conda or `venv`), running Python 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12.

**1. Create and activate an environment** — e.g. with conda, specifying the Python version at creation:

```bash
conda create -c conda-forge -n brainglobe-env python=3.12
```

**2. Install all the tools with pip:**

```bash
pip install brainglobe
```

This fetches all BrainGlobe tools, their Python APIs, and their napari plugins, and installs `napari` itself so you can use the plugins.

**3. Optional — the analysis workflows** (such as `brainmapper`, previously the `cellfinder` CLI):

```bash
pip install brainglobe-workflows>=1.0.0
```

If `brainglobe` isn't already in the environment, this installs it too; otherwise it uses the version you have.

**Updating:**

```bash
pip install brainglobe --upgrade
```

Individual tools can be installed on their own by following each tool's own install instructions, but the docs note that this way a consistent, interoperable set isn't guaranteed — you may hit version or dependency conflicts.

Source: [Installing BrainGlobe](https://github.com/brainglobe/brainglobe.github.io/blob/37ddde1a5d1b5f15cc90649641b80bb14f4c5348/docs/source/documentation/index.md)

Install into a virtual environment (conda or venv) running **Python 3.10, 3.11 or 3.12**:

```bash
conda create -c conda-forge -n brainglobe-env python=3.12
```

Then activate it and install everything with pip:

```bash
pip install brainglobe
```

That fetches all the BrainGlobe tools, their Python APIs, and any napari plugins they have — plus `napari` itself so the plugins work.

**Analysis workflows** (e.g. `brainmapper`, formerly the `cellfinder` CLI) need an extra package:

```bash
pip install brainglobe-workflows>=1.0.0
```

If `brainglobe` isn't already in the environment, this installs it too; otherwise it uses what's there.

**Updating:**

```bash
pip install brainglobe --upgrade
```

The docs note you *can* install each tool individually by following its own install instructions, but then they can't guarantee a consistent, interoperable set — you may hit version or dependency conflicts.

Source: [Installing BrainGlobe](https://github.com/brainglobe/brainglobe.github.io/blob/37ddde1a5d1b5f15cc90649641b80bb14f4c5348/docs/source/documentation/index.md)

question: How do I install photon-mosaic with suite2p support?

tries.answer:
Install it into a virtual environment managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), with the `suite2p` extra. Supported Python versions are 3.12 and 3.13.

```bash
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[suite2p]"
```

Other extras you can add in the same brackets: `widgets` (interactive widget functionality) and `deconvolution` (spike deconvolution with OASIS). The example notebooks need all three:

```bash
uv pip install "photon-mosaic[widgets,suite2p,deconvolution]"
```

Source: [photon-mosaic — Usage](https://github.com/photon-mosaic/photon-mosaic/blob/v0.0.2/docs/source/user-guide.md)


The `suite2p` extra provides suite2p functionality, which is the default for many steps. Two other extras exist: `widgets` (interactive widgets) and `deconvolution` (spike deconvolution with OASIS). If you want to run the example notebooks, they need all three:

